samples.summary: The prompt-drop is an impure side effect during render (mutating `pendingRef`/`promptPathRef`), which is unsafe under this app's concurrent setup and can strand an open dialog whose "Leave" button does nothing
samples.evidence: Lines 191-195 mutate two refs (`pendingRef.current = null; promptPathRef.current = null`) inside the render body, alongside the legal render-phase `setPrompt(null)`. Ref mutation during render is not replayable: if React renders the provider with a location that it does not commit, or restarts/interrupts that render (react-router v7's `BrowserRouter` wraps location updates in `React.startTransition` by default, and App.tsx:15-86 mounts every route through `React.lazy` + `<Suspense>`, so a transition render of a new location routinely suspends before commit), the state update is thrown away while the ref clear is permanent. The committed tree then still has `prompt !== null` (dialog visible, old page still interactive during a suspended transition) but `pendingRef.current === null`, so `leave()` at line 197-203 runs `run?.()` on `undefined`: the dialog closes and the navigation the user just confirmed is silently dropped. The previous `useEffect(stay, [location])` did this work in a committed phase and was not exposed to this. A commit-phase reset keyed on a committed location (or clearing `pendingRef` only from `stay`/`leave`, deriving staleness from the committed `prompt`/path pair) would avoid it.

samples.summary: Comparing only `pathname` keeps a prompt alive across an app redirect that changes the query/hash of the same path, so "Leave" can replay a navigation the user requested from state that no longer exists
samples.evidence: The drop condition `promptPathRef.current !== location.pathname` deliberately ignores search/hash (comment at lines 188-190, test at tests/.../navigation-guard.test.tsx:225). That is defensible for a document rewriting its own query, but the held `run` closure (line 121) also survives an app-issued `replace` to the same pathname with a different search — e.g. a route that re-keys its content off the query string. The dialog then describes a decision taken against content the user is no longer looking at, and confirming replays the original destination. Contained, since the replayed destination is still the one the user clicked, but it is a knowingly narrowed staleness check relative to the `useEffect(stay, [location])` it replaces.

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as described: navigation-guard-provider.tsx:191-195 mutates `pendingRef.current` and `promptPathRef.current` inside the render body next to the render-phase `setPrompt(null)`. Ref mutation is a permanent side effect while the state update is discarded if the render never commits, so the two can desync. The app's setup makes a non-committed render routine: react-router-dom ^7.18.2 `<BrowserRouter>` (package.json:76; App.tsx:95) wraps location updates in `React.startTransition` by default, and every route element is `React.lazy` under `<Suspense>` (App.tsx:15-86, 105-106), with React 19 + StrictMode (package.json:74-75; main.tsx:16-18). A transition render at a new location that suspends leaves the old tree committed and interactive with `prompt !== null` (dialog visible) while the refs are already nulled; `leave()` (lines 197-203) then reads `pendingRef.current === null` and `run?.()` is a no-op, closing the dialog and silently dropping the navigation the user just confirmed. Similarly, an interrupted transition later restarting/committing at the old location commits `setPrompt(null)` with the pending navigation already destroyed. No guard elsewhere restores `pendingRef` — the only other writers are `push` (129-133) and `stay` (170-174) — and the optional call merely prevents a TypeError, not the lost action. This is a broken-invariant/incorrect-state-update issue, squarely in the correctness lane; none of not-present, already-guarded, or out-of-scope applies.

finding.summary: `useEffect(stay, [location, stay])` runs after children's effects, so a prompt raised by a child effect in the same commit is wiped immediately
finding.evidence: The provider itself documents (lines 77-80) that "React runs a child's effects before its parent's" and mirrors `location` during render for exactly that reason. The new auto-stay effect at line 174 ignores the same ordering: on any commit where `location` changed, every child effect runs first, and only then does `stay()` run, nulling `pendingRef` and `setPrompt(null)`. A child that issues a guarded `push` from a mount/update effect in that commit (a redirect rendered as `<Navigate to=... />` without `replace`, e.g. PrivateRoute.tsx:32, or any `navigate()` inside a `useEffect`) will have its prompt raised and then silently destroyed in the same commit — the navigation neither happens nor is offered to the user; the click/redirect is swallowed with no UI at all. The effect cannot distinguish "the app navigated past this prompt" from "this prompt was just created during this commit".

verdict.reason: The finding asserts a `useEffect(stay, [location, stay])` at navigation-guard-provider.tsx:174. No such effect exists: the provider imports only useCallback/useContext/useMemo/useRef/useState (lines 1-8) — `useEffect` is not imported, and a grep of the navigation-guard directory finds `useEffect` in the provider only inside a comment (line 183). Lines 170-174 are the `stay` useCallback with an empty dep array. The location-change drop is instead decided during render (lines 191-195) via `promptPathRef.current !== location.pathname`, where `promptPathRef` is stamped at push time from the render-mirrored `locationRef` (lines 80-82, 131) — so a prompt raised by a child effect in a commit where location already changed records the new pathname and survives the resulting render, which is exactly the scenario the finding claims is broken; the comment at lines 183-190 documents this render-time placement as the deliberate avoidance of the child-before-parent effect-ordering hazard. The cited bypassing call site is also wrong: PrivateRoute.tsx:36 is `<Navigate to="/login" replace />` (PublicRoute.tsx:24 likewise), and only `push` is guarded (line 163; `replace` is a straight passthrough at line 164), so those redirects never raise a prompt.

searchedFor: grep for <Navigate / replace: true across packages/frontend/src
finding.summary: The premise behind leaving `replace` unguarded is false: the app's auth redirects use push `<Navigate>`, so they are routed through the guard
finding.evidence: navigation-guard-provider.tsx:148-155 justifies guarding only `push` on the claim that app-initiated redirects — "`PrivateRoute` sending you to /login" — are `replace`. They are not: `PrivateRoute.tsx:32` renders `<Navigate to="/login" />` and `PublicRoute.tsx:21` renders `<Navigate to="/" />`, both without `replace`, and `<Navigate>` calls `navigate()` from an effect, i.e. `navigator.push`. If that redirect fires while a guard is still registered, it hits the guarded path and a "Stay" swallows it permanently — precisely the stranding failure the comment says the push/replace split avoids. It only escapes today by depending on React running the deleted editor subtree's passive cleanup (which unregisters the guard) before `<Navigate>`'s effect in the same commit — an ordering the code neither states nor enforces.

verdict.reason: The finding's central factual claim is false in this working tree. It asserts `PrivateRoute.tsx:32` renders `<Navigate to="/login" />` and `PublicRoute.tsx:21` renders `<Navigate to="/" />` "both without `replace`". In fact PrivateRoute.tsx:36 is `<Navigate to="/login" replace />` (lines 32-35 are a comment explaining that it must be a replace so NavigationGuardProvider cannot refuse it), and PublicRoute.tsx:24 is `<Navigate to="/" replace />` with the same rationale at lines 21-23. A repo-wide grep for `Navigate` confirms every app-issued `<Navigate>` redirect carries `replace` (home-or-redirect.tsx:26, document-detail.tsx:863, board-detail.tsx:252, file-detail.tsx:242 and :247, notes-detail.tsx:369, docs-detail.tsx:342, slides-detail.tsx:947). Because these redirects go through `navigator.replace` (navigation-guard-provider.tsx:164, unguarded passthrough) and never the guarded `push` (lines 120-138), the described stranding path — a "Stay" permanently swallowing an auth redirect — is not reachable, and the alleged reliance on effect-cleanup ordering does not arise. The provider comment at lines 151-161 states this as an invariant the code currently upholds at every call site.
